newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's exiled king to meet President Berisha.
newsitem.headline: Albania's exiled king to meet President Berisha.

text.p: Albania's King Leka prepared to meet rival head of state President Sali Berisha on Friday after calling for a restoration of the monarchy when he returned to his troubled homeland after 58 years in exile.
"This will be an historic meeting," said Guri Durollari, the leader of the royalist Legality Movement.
"We have worked very hard to bring the king back home."
The bespectacled, grey-haired king, who at 2.05 metres (six feet five inches) dwarfs most of his countrymen, will meet Berisha at the presidential palace around midday, he said.
The meeting, the most important since his return on Saturday, will be the first between the two men.

King Leka, who sees himself as a unifying factor in a country shattered by violence and lawlessness since dubious savings schemes collapsed earlier this year, was only days old when his father, King Zog, fled with his family in 1939.
The meeting took place in Tirana as more French and Italian troops arrived in the nearby port of Durres in the build-up of a U.N.-backed multinational force sent to secure aid convoys.
Some 2,000 Albanians treated King Leka to a wild welcome when he flew by private plane from South Africa.
Dozens broke through police cordons and jumped onto his limousine while supporters chanted "Long Live King Leka" and waved red-and-black Albanian flags.
The rapturous reception for the man who says he is still king under the pre-communist 1928 constitution contrasted starkly with the popular anger directed against Berisha.
Rebels who control much of the south have demanded Berisha's resignation after two months of chaos which have claimed nearly 300 lives.

Berisha, a northerner, has agreed to hold an early general election by the end of June. He has brought the opposition Socialists into government with his own rightist Democratic Party, but rebels say they will not give up until Berisha goes.
International mediator Franz Vranitzky said on Thursday that parties had agreed they wanted to hold the vote on June 29 but first had to find consensus on other issues.
The self-styled rebel "salvation committees" remain the thorniest issue, said Vranitzky, an envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Parties are divided on how to deal with them, as well as on what political system should be used for the election and how the constitution should be re-drafted.

King Leka says he favours a referendum to allow Albanians to choose between a monarchy or a republic. The monarchy was abolished under a post-war constitution but King Leka says the people were never consulted.

A contingent of more than 700 Greek soldiers was expected to land in Durres later in the day and to travel by land to the port of Vlore to become the first sizeable contingent deployed in the rebel-held south.

The 6,000-strong force, which also includes troops from Turkey, Spain, Romania, Denmark and Austria, is expected to become fully operational within three weeks. The first major humanitarian aid delivery is expected by the weekend.
King Leka was due to meet moslem leaders after his talks with Berisha. Friday is a moslem holiday and the king was born into the faith.
On Sunday, he plans to visit the remote mountain village of Burgajet, north of Tirana, where his father was born.
